title: Off-Manifold Collapse in Guided Protein Language Models

paper.title:
Off-Manifold Collapse in Guided Protein Language
Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract Protein language models are widely used priors for protein sequence design, and
a growing body of work controls them at inference time as an alternative to
fine-tuning. Such guidance faces a dilemma: mild enough to preserve natural
activation statistics, it barely moves the property; strong enough to move it,
the generations become progressively harder to fold. We show the failure has a
specific and cheaply detectable signature, an off-manifold collapse of the
model’s own representations. Guided activations fall toward a region
statistically indistinguishable from random amino-acid input, and the sequences
degenerate to low complexity, yet the property oracle being optimized can
still score these generations as a success. The optimized oracle can therefore
fail to witness the collapse and, for solubility, can actively reward it,
whereas structure and composition expose the failure. Because the failure is already visible in a
finished candidate, we detect it at the output rather than modify the generator.
We introduce a cheap density prior over natural protein activations and keep
only the candidates that remain typical under it, a training-free post-hoc step
we call Mahalanobis filtering . At matched guidance settings it improves
both the property score and the structural plausibility of the sequences it
keeps at negligible cost, without touching the generator, and transfers across
different guidance methods.
We release the activation statistic at https://huggingface.co/Shuibai12138/off-manifold-collapse-plm .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Pretrained protein language models (PLMs) such as ESM-2 ( 17 ) , ESM3 ( 9 ) , ProGen ( 20 ) , and ProtGPT2 ( 5 ) are widely used priors for protein sequence design, and a growing body of work controls them at inference time rather than by fine-tuning: some follow the gradient of a trained property model through the generator ( 2 ; 8 ; 29 ; 30 ) , others reshape the token distribution at decoding ( 4 ; 1 ) , and activation steering edits the hidden states themselves. Steering is among the most attractive of these: transplanted from the control of large language models ( 27 ) , it adds a direction computed from high- and low-property reference sequences to the residual stream during masked decoding and obtains sequences the oracle scores above the reference set ( 10 ) ; Section 2 gives the mechanism. Steering requires neither gradients through the property model nor weight updates. We study it as the primary intervention and use predictor-gradient guidance as a mechanistically distinct transfer test. Aggressive inference-time control nevertheless carries a structural cost. Other controllers report the same tension from the opposite side ( 4 ; 1 ) . Logit-difference amplification addresses the degraded sequence properties and distributional similarity caused by activation steering ( 4 ) , while iterative lookback Monte-Carlo sampling targets steering-induced diversity loss ( 1 ) . These studies establish that the degradation is real and recognized, but each treats it as a reason to replace steering; neither directly characterizes its representation-space signature. Figure 1 shows what it looks like in a single pair of generations: pushed hard enough to move the property, steering makes ESM-2 emit a glycine homopolymer that the solubility oracle rates as almost certainly soluble ( 0.99 0.99 ) while ESMFold confidence falls to 0.35 0.35 . The optimized oracle prefers the degenerate sequence, so the failure can only be read from referees outside the steering objective. We therefore ask: What happens to a protein language model’s representations when steering is pushed hard enough to move the property, and can the resulting failure be mitigated after generation? In this work, we make the following contributions: • A characterization of the failure as off-manifold collapse . Across both solubility and thermostability steering, the representations become less typical and ESMFold pLDDT decreases. However, the property-oracle score does not necessarily decrease at the same time. Therefore, the property score alone is not a reliable indicator of successful steering (Section 3 ). • Mahalanobis-filtered steering , a training-free selection layer. A χ 2 \chi^{2} -inspired one-sided typicality test over natural activations that improves the property–structure trade-off at matched settings and costs almost nothing, with a precise account of its scope (Section 4 , Appendix H ) and a public release of priors, statistics, and code. Figure 1: The failure mode in one pair of generations (solubility, ESM-2 650M). The unguided sample uses all 20 20 amino acids, folds confidently, and scores low; under strong all-layer steering the model emits a glycine homopolymer that the steering objective rates as almost certainly soluble. The optimized oracle prefers the degenerate sequence, whereas structure and composition expose it. The population-level property–structure trade-off is reported in Appendix B .

sections.heading: Protein language models.
sections.text: A protein is a string over an alphabet of 20 20 amino acids whose folded structure determines its function and properties such as solubility or thermostability. Trained on databases of natural proteins, a protein language model is a generic prior over “protein-like” sequences whose activations encode structure and function ( 25 ; 21 ) : ESM-2 ( 17 ) is a masked language model trained on UniRef ( 26 ) , and we work with its 650M variant. The family spans masked encoders ( 17 ; 3 ) , autoregressive generators ( 20 ; 22 ; 5 ) , discrete-diffusion generators ( 29 ) , instruction-tuned variants ( 19 ) , and multimodal generative models over sequence, structure, and function ( 9 ) . Generation is by iterative masked decoding : from a reference sequence, positions are repeatedly masked and resampled from the model until every position has been re-predicted ( 10 ) .

sections.heading: Activation steering.
sections.text: Activation steering edits a model’s hidden states at inference time: one fixed direction is added to the residual stream, with no weight update, a technique developed for controlling large language models ( 27 ; 16 ; 24 ; 31 ) . The direction is typically a difference of means between the activations of two contrasting example sets, and Huang et al. ( 10 ) apply it to PLMs. Write h ℓ ​ ( s ) h_{\ell}(s) for the layer- ℓ \ell activation of a reference sequence s s , and let ℋ \mathcal{H} and ℒ \mathcal{L} be reference sets labeled high and low for the target property. The steering vector, and the update it makes to the residual stream x x at that layer in every forward pass of masked decoding, are v ℓ = 1 | ℋ | ​ ∑ s ∈ ℋ h ℓ ​ ( s ) − 1 | ℒ | ​ ∑ s ∈ ℒ h ℓ ​ ( s ) , x ← ( x + α ​ v ℓ ) ​ ∥ x ∥ ∥ x + α ​ v ℓ ∥ , v_{\ell}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{H}|}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{H}}h_{\ell}(s)\;-\;\frac{1}{|\mathcal{L}|}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{L}}h_{\ell}(s),\qquad x\;\leftarrow\;\big(x+\alpha v_{\ell}\big)\,\frac{\lVert x\rVert}{\lVert x+\alpha v_{\ell}\rVert}, (1) where α \alpha sets the strength and the rescaling preserves the norm of x x . We use all layer injection ( allL ) throughout the main experiments and perform a single layer sweep injection for an auxiliary analysis. Preserving the raw norm in Eq. 1 , however, does not preserve the per-channel whitened profile, so the steered activations can still leave the model’s typical activation region, as measured in Section 3 .

sections.heading: Predictor-gradient guidance.
sections.text: As a mechanistically distinct controller, we also guide masked decoding using the gradient of the property oracle. At each round, the activation is moved by a fraction η \eta of its norm along the normalized gradient, producing an input-dependent direction. Because the same oracle both defines this update and reports the property score, its increase is expected.

sections.heading: How a generated protein is judged.
sections.text: We evaluate generated proteins along two complementary axes. First, a property oracle estimates the intended functional shift: a solubility classifier ( 15 ) or a T m T_{m} regressor ( 11 ) , each trained on frozen ESM-2 features. These predictors define the steering objective, but fitness models become less reliable under distant extrapolation and vary across protein families ( 6 ; 23 ) . Second, we use ESMFold pLDDT ( 17 ) as a proxy for structural plausibility, reporting it over populations rather than treating any individual prediction as definitive. AlphaFold confidence provides an alternative ( 14 ) ; ESMFold’s MSA-free inference makes population-scale evaluation tractable. Neither axis replaces experimental validation: computational metrics do not by themselves establish activity ( 13 ) ; experimental studies of generated proteins and closed-loop methods rely on wet-lab feedback ( 28 ; 12 ) ; our method remains a computational pre-screen.

sections.heading: 3 Diagnosing Steering-Induced Collapse
sections.text: Figures 2 – 3 use the released solubility difficulty splits solely for diagnostic visualization. sol_hard contains low-solubility references, whereas sol_easy contains moderately soluble references; see Appendix A for details. Figure 2: Property is bought with structure ( sol_hard , α = 0 \alpha=0 is unguided) Increasing steering strength raises predicted solubility overall but sharply reduces ESMFold pLDDT; bands are standard errors.

sections.heading: Property is bought with structure.
sections.text: Figure 2 reveals a systematic trade-off: as steering strengthens, predicted solubility rises overall from 0.12 0.12 to 0.38 0.38 , while ESMFold pLDDT falls sharply from 0.66 0.66 to 0.32 0.32 . Structural confidence deteriorates before a substantial property shift appears: by α = 0.2 \alpha=0.2 , pLDDT has already fallen to 0.60 0.60 while predicted solubility remains near its unguided level, showing that the degradation is gradual rather than confined to extreme steering. Because the oracle measures a predicted property shift rather than experimental validation, we evaluate every setting jointly by its target-property score and pLDDT, and judge our remedy by whether it recovers structural confidence without sacrificing the achieved shift; full sweep results are provided in Appendix B .

sections.text: Natural moments ( μ , σ 2 ) (\mu,\sigma^{2}) are estimated once from UniRef50, reused throughout, and detailed in Appendix A .

sections.heading: What collapses: the representation.
sections.text: To test whether the output-level loss of structural confidence has an activation-space counterpart, we inspect the generator’s own hidden states. We use a diagonal Mahalanobis score because the dominant failure is radial: as steering strengthens, the standardized per-channel activations contract toward the UniRef50 mean, which this score measures directly. Let h ∈ ℝ L × D h\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times D} denote the interior-token layer-17 activations of a candidate sequence, where D = 1280 D=1280 for ESM-2 650M, and let ( μ , σ 2 ) (\mu,\sigma^{2}) denote the per-channel mean and variance of natural layer-17 activations, estimated once from UniRef50 ( 26 ) . We measure Mahal 2 ​ ( h ) = 1 L ​ ∑ i = 1 L ∑ d = 1 D ( h i , d − μ d σ d ) 2 . \mathrm{Mahal}^{2}(h)=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=1}^{L}\sum_{d=1}^{D}\left(\frac{h_{i,d}-\mu_{d}}{\sigma_{d}}\right)^{2}. (2) This construction adopts a deliberately simplified working model: natural activations are approximately Gaussian after per-channel standardization, and cross-channel covariance is ignored. We do not treat this diagonal Gaussian as an exact model of the latent distribution; rather, it provides a cheap, calibrated statistic of radial typicality. Under this model, the per-token sum has reference distribution χ 2 ​ ( D ) \chi^{2}(D) with mean D D . Because token positions are correlated, however, the sequence-level average is not itself χ 2 ​ ( D ) \chi^{2}(D) , so we interpret it against the empirical unguided distribution (mean 1226 1226 , s.d. 317 317 ). Figure 3 shows that the score falls from 1232 1232 to approximately 600 600 as steering strengthens, approaching the random-amino-acid reference of 604 604 . On the all-layer sweep in Figure 2 , Mahal 2 \mathrm{Mahal}^{2} likewise falls from 1226 1226 to 642 642 as pLDDT falls from 0.66 0.66 to 0.32 0.32 . These results motivate using the score as an activation-space indicator of the collapse associated with reduced structural confidence. The failure is a collapse toward the channel-wise mean, which is what a diagonal-Gaussian typicality test detects.

sections.heading: The same inward collapse appears under predictor-gradient guidance.
sections.text: On the same UniRef50 references, increasing η \eta moves populations inward for both properties: Mahal 2 \mathrm{Mahal}^{2} and ESMFold pLDDT decrease at every guidance strength. The property increase is not independent evidence because the same oracle supplies the gradient and score. Their synchronized decline shows that inward collapse extends beyond fixed-vector steering; filter transfer is evaluated in Section 5 .

sections.heading: 4 Mahalanobis-Filtered Steering
sections.text: The diagnosis in Section 3 identifies a dominant inward failure mode: guided activations contract toward the channel-wise mean and fall below the natural shell. Because generator-side mitigations were not consistent across properties (Appendix G ), we instead apply a one-sided post-hoc veto to completed candidates. Given the score in Eq. 2 , we accept a candidate iff Mahal 2 ​ ( h ) ≥ D − k ​ 2 ​ D , \mathrm{Mahal}^{2}(h)\geq D-k\sqrt{2D}, (3) where we set k = 1 k=1 once and use the resulting threshold, 1229 1229 for D = 1280 D=1280 , unchanged across tasks, properties, reference sets, and guidance mechanisms. The rule is χ 2 \chi^{2} -inspired rather than an exact sequence-level quantile because token positions are correlated; Appendix E gives its calibration and sensitivity. It is one-sided because it targets inward collapse; outward extremes are outside its scope and reported in Appendix C . The filter operates only on completed sequences and does not modify decoding. Scoring requires no additional learned model beyond ESM-2: one forward pass of the completed sequence, followed by per-channel standardization and summation using two stored 1280 1280 -dimensional moment vectors. Because it reads only the final activations, the same filter attaches unchanged to all-layer steering, predictor-gradient guidance, and unguided generation. Every comparison below is between a generated pool and the subset selected from that same pool by Eq. 3 ; the filter is a selector, not a standalone generator.

sections.heading: The detector transfers across guidance mechanisms.
sections.text: The result is not restricted to steering. We apply the same method to predictor gradient guidance, without retraining or recalibration. Across both properties and three guidance strengths, increasing the guidance step moves the population inward, and filtering raises mean pLDDT by 0.144 0.144 – 0.175 0.175 in all six UniRef50 guidance pools, with every paired-bootstrap interval excluding zero. The oracle increase under gradient guidance is not treated as independent evidence, because the same oracle supplies the guidance gradient. Complete results, including the family reference pool, are reported in Appendix D . This transfer supports robustness across properties and intervention mechanisms on a broad UniRef50 background. It does not imply that the one-sided rule detects every possible failure of extreme steering: outward collapse remains outside the regime targeted by Eq. 3 .

sections.heading: A cheap statistic suffices.
sections.text: Across 4,400 4{,}400 sequences, the diagonal statistic agrees with the exact flow NLL across broad regimes (pooled Spearman r = 0.82 r=0.82 ), but heterogeneous within-setting correlations do not imply identical selections. The exact NLL used for this comparison costs ≈ 3 {\approx}3 s per sequence and requires a 1.3 1.3 GB model; its approximate flow-residual readout costs 283 283 ms, whereas the Mahalanobis costs 34 34 ms and stores only 10 10 KB (Appendix F ).

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: Effective activation steering can drive ESM-2’s representations off the natural typicality shell into a region shared with random amino-acid input, where a learned oracle may still read the result as a success. Because that signature survives in a finished candidate, a 10 10 KB one-sided typicality test recovers the sequences a steered pool has left on the manifold, at matched settings and negligible cost. It selects rather than projects, so it helps only while a viable tail remains; Appendix H gives the full scope and limitations.

sections.heading: Model and decoding.
sections.text: All experiments use ESM-2 650M ( esm2_t33_650M_UR50D ) ( 17 ) with token dropout disabled. Generation is iterative masked decoding from a reference sequence: ten rounds, each masking 10 % 10\% of the positions not yet resampled , one forward pass per round, with replacements sampled by top- p p ( p = 0.9 p{=}0.9 , temperature 1.0 1.0 ) restricted to the 20 20 canonical amino acids. Because the candidate pool shrinks each round, every position is re-predicted exactly once. Batch size is 1 1 . Seeds are fixed per sequence, so matched methods share mask schedules.

sections.heading: Reference sets.
sections.text: Unless noted, each (reference set, property, setting) contains 128 128 generations. global is a property-unconditioned draw of UniRef50 sequences of length 50 50 – 256 256 ; both properties share its references and seeds. lyso is reconstructed from the property-thresholded lysozyme-like files released by Huang et al. ( 10 ) , excluding the 200 200 steering-vector examples, and is therefore neither property-unconditioned nor a released generation set. The diagnostic-only sol_hard and sol_easy splits are likewise property-conditioned: Figure 2 uses the low-solubility split to expose the property–structure trade-off, while Figure 3 uses single-layer steering on the medium split to isolate activation collapse under single-layer steering. Main-text evaluation uses global , with lyso reported as a family-derived replication.

sections.heading: Oracles.
sections.text: Both property predictors are our own retrains of the published recipe, a frozen ESM-2 650M mean-pooled feature extractor with an MLP head, because the original checkpoints were not public. Solubility is trained on DeepSol ( 15 ) and reaches test accuracy 0.651 0.651 ; thermostability is trained on Meltome ( 11 ) median T m T_{m} and reaches test Spearman 0.687 0.687 . Both are weaker than the figures reported for the originals ( 0.708 0.708 and 0.76 0.76 respectively), and the thermostability predictor was trained without redundancy reduction, so its held-out figure is if anything optimistic. Every property number in this paper is this oracle’s, and the oracle is in silico throughout: no experimental validation is claimed.

sections.heading: Referee.
sections.text: Structural plausibility is ESMFold ( 17 ) mean per-residue pLDDT at one recycle.

sections.heading: Choice of activation readout layer.
sections.text: We use layer 17 17 throughout as a fixed activation readout. ESM-2 650M has 33 33 transformer blocks, making layer 17 17 its middle layer. This choice also has precedent in activation-distribution modelling: Luo et al. ( 18 ) train their activation model on the middle-most layer of both Llama-1B (layer 7 7 ) and Llama-8B (layer 15 15 ), while exploring multi-layer modelling separately. Layer 17 17 is also functionally informative in our setting: steering it alone shifts predicted solubility from 0.263 0.263 to 0.341 0.341 while largely preserving pLDDT ( 0.662 0.662 to 0.635 0.635 ; Table 9 ). We therefore estimate its natural moments once from UniRef50 and use them throughout. Affiliation: University of Wisconsin–Madison Xinchi Liu 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: University of Wisconsin–Madison Fred Zhangzhi Peng Affiliation: Duke University Zhihan Yang Affiliation: Cornell University Shutong Wu Affiliation: University of Wisconsin–Madison Yingzi Ma Affiliation: University of Wisconsin–Madison Jiawei Zhang Affiliation: University of Wisconsin–Madison Abstract Protein language models are widely used priors for protein sequence design, and a growing body of work controls them at inference time as an alternative to fine-tuning. Such guidance faces a dilemma: mild enough to preserve natural activation statistics, it barely moves the property; strong enough to move it, the generations become progressively harder to fold. We show the failure has a specific and cheaply detectable signature, an off-manifold collapse of the model’s own representations. Guided activations fall toward a region statistically indistinguishable from random amino-acid input, and the sequences degenerate to low complexity, yet the property oracle being optimized can still score these generations as a success. The optimized oracle can therefore fail to witness the collapse and, for solubility, can actively reward it, whereas structure and composition expose the failure. Because the failure is already visible in a finished candidate, we detect it at the output rather than modify the generator. We introduce a cheap density prior over natural protein activations and keep only the candidates that remain typical under it, a training-free post-hoc step we call Mahalanobis filtering . At matched guidance settings it improves both the property score and the structural plausibility of the sequences it keeps at negligible cost, without touching the generator, and transfers across different guidance methods. We release the activation statistic at https://huggingface.co/Shuibai12138/off-manifold-collapse-plm . 1 Introduction Pretrained protein language models (PLMs) such as ESM-2 ( 17 ) , ESM3 ( 9 ) , ProGen ( 20 ) , and ProtGPT2 ( 5 ) are widely used priors for protein sequence design, and a growing body of work controls them at inference time rather than by fine-tuning: some follow the gradient of a trained property model through the generator ( 2 ; 8 ; 29 ; 30 ) , others reshape the token distribution at decoding ( 4 ; 1 ) , and activation steering edits the hidden states themselves. Steering is among the most attractive of these: transplanted from the control of large language models ( 27 ) , it adds a direction computed from high- and low-property reference sequences to the residual stream during masked decoding and obtains sequences the oracle scores above the reference set ( 10 ) ; Section 2 gives the mechanism. Steering requires neither gradients through the property model nor weight updates. We study it as the primary intervention and use predictor-gradient guidance as a mechanistically distinct transfer test. Aggressive inference-time control nevertheless carries a structural cost. Other controllers report the same tension from the opposite side ( 4 ; 1 ) . Logit-difference amplification addresses the degraded sequence properties and distributional similarity caused by activation steering ( 4 ) , while iterative lookback Monte-Carlo sampling targets steering-induced diversity loss ( 1 ) . These studies establish that the degradation is real and recognized, but each treats it as a reason to replace steering; neither directly characterizes its representation-space signature. Figure 1 shows what it looks like in a single pair of generations: pushed hard enough to move the property, steering makes ESM-2 emit a glycine homopolymer that the solubility oracle rates as almost certainly soluble ( 0.99 0.99 ) while ESMFold confidence falls to 0.35 0.35 . The optimized oracle prefers the degenerate sequence, so the failure can only be read from referees outside the steering objective. We therefore ask: What happens to a protein language model’s representations when steering is pushed hard enough to move the property, and can the resulting failure be mitigated after generation? In this work, we make the following contributions: • A characterization of the failure as off-manifold collapse . Across both solubility and thermostability steering, the representations become less typical and ESMFold pLDDT decreases. However, the property-oracle score does not necessarily decrease at the same time. Therefore, the property score alone is not a reliable indicator of successful steering (Section 3 ). • Mahalanobis-filtered steering , a training-free selection layer. A χ 2 \chi^{2} -inspired one-sided typicality test over natural activations that improves the property–structure trade-off at matched settings and costs almost nothing, with a precise account of its scope (Section 4 , Appendix H ) and a public release of priors, statistics, and code. Figure 1: The failure mode in one pair of generations (solubility, ESM-2 650M). The unguided sample uses all 20 20 amino acids, folds confidently, and scores low; under strong all-layer steering the model emits a glycine homopolymer that the steering objective rates as almost certainly soluble. The optimized oracle prefers the degenerate sequence, whereas structure and composition expose it. The population-level property–structure trade-off is reported in Appendix B . 2 Background Protein language models. A protein is a string over an alphabet of 20 20 amino acids whose folded structure determines its function and properties such as solubility or thermostability. Trained on databases of natural proteins, a protein language model is a generic prior over “protein-like” sequences whose activations encode structure and function ( 25 ; 21 ) : ESM-2 ( 17 ) is a masked language model trained on UniRef ( 26 ) , and we work with its 650M variant. The family spans masked encoders ( 17 ; 3 ) , autoregressive generators ( 20 ; 22 ; 5 ) , discrete-diffusion generators ( 29 ) , instruction-tuned variants ( 19 ) , and multimodal generative models over sequence, structure, and function ( 9 ) . Generation is by iterative masked decoding : from a reference sequence, positions are repeatedly masked and resampled from the model until every position has been re-predicted ( 10 ) . Activation steering. Activation steering edits a model’s hidden states at inference time: one fixed direction is added to the residual stream, with no weight update, a technique developed for controlling large language models ( 27 ; 16 ; 24 ; 31 ) . The direction is typically a difference of means between the activations of two contrasting example sets, and Huang et al. ( 10 ) apply it to PLMs. Write h ℓ ​ ( s ) h_{\ell}(s) for the layer- ℓ \ell activation of a reference sequence s s , and let ℋ \mathcal{H} and ℒ \mathcal{L} be reference sets labeled high and low for the target property. The steering vector, and the update it makes to the residual stream x x at that layer in every forward pass of masked decoding, are v ℓ = 1 | ℋ | ​ ∑ s ∈ ℋ h ℓ ​ ( s ) − 1 | ℒ | ​ ∑ s ∈ ℒ h ℓ ​ ( s ) , x ← ( x + α ​ v ℓ ) ​ ∥ x ∥ ∥ x + α ​ v ℓ ∥ , v_{\ell}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{H}|}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{H}}h_{\ell}(s)\;-\;\frac{1}{|\mathcal{L}|}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{L}}h_{\ell}(s),\qquad x\;\leftarrow\;\big(x+\alpha v_{\ell}\big)\,\frac{\lVert x\rVert}{\lVert x+\alpha v_{\ell}\rVert}, (1) where α \alpha sets the strength and the rescaling preserves the norm of x x . We use all layer injection ( allL ) throughout the main experiments and perform a single layer sweep injection for an auxiliary analysis. Preserving the raw norm in Eq. 1 , however, does not preserve the per-channel whitened profile, so the steered activations can still leave the model’s typical activation region, as measured in Section 3 . Predictor-gradient guidance. As a mechanistically distinct controller, we also guide masked decoding using the gradient of the property oracle. At each round, the activation is moved by a fraction η \eta of its norm along the normalized gradient, producing an input-dependent direction. Because the same oracle both defines this update and reports the property score, its increase is expected. How a generated protein is judged. We evaluate generated proteins along two complementary axes. First, a property oracle estimates the intended functional shift: a solubility classifier ( 15 ) or a T m T_{m} regressor ( 11 ) , each trained on frozen ESM-2 features. These predictors define the steering objective, but fitness models become less reliable under distant extrapolation and vary across protein families ( 6 ; 23 ) . Second, we use ESMFold pLDDT ( 17 ) as a proxy for structural plausibility, reporting it over populations rather than treating any individual prediction as definitive. AlphaFold confidence provides an alternative ( 14 ) ; ESMFold’s MSA-free inference makes population-scale evaluation tractable. Neither axis replaces experimental validation: computational metrics do not by themselves establish activity ( 13 ) ; experimental studies of generated proteins and closed-loop methods rely on wet-lab feedback ( 28 ; 12 ) ; our method remains a computational pre-screen. 3 Diagnosing Steering-Induced Collapse Figures 2 – 3 use the released solubility difficulty splits solely for diagnostic visualization. sol_hard contains low-solubility references, whereas sol_easy contains moderately soluble references; see Appendix A for details. Figure 2: Property is bought with structure ( sol_hard , α = 0 \alpha=0 is unguided) Increasing steering strength raises predicted solubility overall but sharply reduces ESMFold pLDDT; bands are standard errors. Property is bought with structure. Figure 2 reveals a systematic trade-off: as steering strengthens, predicted solubility rises overall from 0.12 0.12 to 0.38 0.38 , while ESMFold pLDDT falls sharply from 0.66 0.66 to 0.32 0.32 . Structural confidence deteriorates before a substantial property shift appears: by α = 0.2 \alpha=0.2 , pLDDT has already fallen to 0.60 0.60 while predicted solubility remains near its unguided level, showing that the degradation is gradual rather than confined to extreme steering. Because the oracle measures a predicted property shift rather than experimental validation, we evaluate every setting jointly by its target-property score and pLDDT, and judge our remedy by whether it recovers structural confidence without sacrificing the achieved shift; full sweep results are provided in Appendix B . Reference statistics. Natural moments ( μ , σ 2 ) (\mu,\sigma^{2}) are estimated once from UniRef50, reused throughout, and detailed in Appendix A . What collapses: the representation. To test whether the output-level loss of structural confidence has an activation-space counterpart, we inspect the generator’s own hidden states. We use a diagonal Mahalanobis score because the dominant failure is radial: as steering strengthens, the standardized per-channel activations contract toward the UniRef50 mean, which this score measures directly. Let h ∈ ℝ L × D h\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times D} denote the interior-token layer-17 activations of a candidate sequence, where D = 1280 D=1280 for ESM-2 650M, and let ( μ , σ 2 ) (\mu,\sigma^{2}) denote the per-channel mean and variance of natural layer-17 activations, estimated once from UniRef50 ( 26 ) . We measure Mahal 2 ​ ( h ) = 1 L ​ ∑ i = 1 L ∑ d = 1 D ( h i , d − μ d σ d ) 2 . \mathrm{Mahal}^{2}(h)=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=1}^{L}\sum_{d=1}^{D}\left(\frac{h_{i,d}-\mu_{d}}{\sigma_{d}}\right)^{2}. (2) This construction adopts a deliberately simplified working model: natural activations are approximately Gaussian after per-channel standardization, and cross-channel covariance is ignored. We do not treat this diagonal Gaussian as an exact model of the latent distribution; rather, it provides a cheap, calibrated statistic of radial typicality. Under this model, the per-token sum has reference distribution χ 2 ​ ( D ) \chi^{2}(D) with mean D D . Because token positions are correlated, however, the sequence-level average is not itself χ 2 ​ ( D ) \chi^{2}(D) , so we interpret it against the empirical unguided distribution (mean 1226 1226 , s.d. 317 317 ). Figure 3 shows that the score falls from 1232 1232 to approximately 600 600 as steering strengthens, approaching the random-amino-acid reference of 604 604 . On the all-layer sweep in Figure 2 , Mahal 2 \mathrm{Mahal}^{2} likewise falls from 1226 1226 to 642 642 as pLDDT falls from 0.66 0.66 to 0.32 0.32 . These results motivate using the score as an activation-space indicator of the collapse associated with reduced structural confidence. Appendix F validates the diagonal approximation against a flexible flow-based density model fitted to the same activations. The failure is a collapse toward the channel-wise mean, which is what a diagonal-Gaussian typicality test detects. The same inward collapse appears under predictor-gradient guidance. On the same UniRef50 references, increasing η \eta moves populations inward for both properties: Mahal 2 \mathrm{Mahal}^{2} and ESMFold pLDDT decrease at every guidance strength. The property increase is not independent evidence because the same oracle supplies the gradient and score. Their synchronized decline shows that inward collapse extends beyond fixed-vector steering; filter transfer is evaluated in Section 5 . 4 Mahalanobis-Filtered Steering The diagnosis in Section 3 identifies a dominant inward failure mode: guided activations contract toward the channel-wise mean and fall below the natural shell. Because generator-side mitigations were not consistent across properties (Appendix G ), we instead apply a one-sided post-hoc veto to completed candidates. Given the score in Eq. 2 , we accept a candidate iff Mahal 2 ​ ( h ) ≥ D − k ​ 2 ​ D , \mathrm{Mahal}^{2}(h)\geq D-k\sqrt{2D}, (3) where we set k = 1 k=1 once and use the resulting threshold, 1229 1229 for D = 1280 D=1280 , unchanged across tasks, properties, reference sets, and guidance mechanisms. The rule is χ 2 \chi^{2} -inspired rather than an exact sequence-level quantile because token positions are correlated; Appendix E gives its calibration and sensitivity. It is one-sided because it targets inward collapse; outward extremes are outside its scope and reported in Appendix C . The filter operates only on completed sequences and does not modify decoding.
